catalog_quote: Multisyllabic words can show initial stress, as in (7), or final stress, as in (8). Many of the words that fall into the latter category contain an initial vowel only, suggestive of the sesquisyllabic syllable type often associated with Austroasiatic languages (Matisoff 1973); however, instead of a schwa, this vowel is a fully realised low, back vowel. ... Both Dzongkha and the East Bodish languages also have (exclusively) word-initial stress. Neither word-final stress nor glottalized syllables are found in adjacent languages, to our knowledge ... Note, importantly, that the stress pattern in this word is different than the stress pattern of the other kinship terms. audit.reasoning: Quote check: every clause of the deciding quotation and the secondary 2016 passages was found verbatim in the held PDFs at the stated locators (Hyslop 2023 p.111 paras 4-5 and exx. 5-8; Hyslop 2016 p.86 sec.3.1, sec.4 kinship paragraph, sec.5, fn.8). The classification (lexical stress, initial or final, no weight/positional rule) matches what the sources say and what the 18 stress-marked forms in Hyslop 2016 show. The deciding source is the most recent first-hand statement by the language's principal documenter, but it is a 2-page impressionistic conference abstract for a moribund ~500-speaker language whose prosody the author herself calls underdescribed, so 'adequate' rather than 'well-sourced'. downloaded now: van Driem 1995 (open, Minpaku repository) - its phonology section (p.235) covers vowels and register tone only, silent on stress. not yet obtained and not fetchable: Gerber 2020 LTBA (paywalled, r

sources.note: Only dedicated phonology article treating Black Mountain Mönpa (32 pp, based largely on van Driem's data from a different village than Hyslop's Rukha); our classification rests on a 2-page abstract plus a documentation sketch, and Gerber may state a stress/word-prosody pattern (or sesquisyllabic analysis) that refines the initial-vs-final lexical coding.
